newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU makes good threat on textile liberalisation.
newsitem.headline: EU makes good threat on textile liberalisation.

text.p: The European Commission on Wednesday made good a threat to include only token products in a second phase of textile trade liberalisation when it unveiled a list of items to be freed next year.

Although the volume of goods exceeds the European Union's obligations, it includes products such as ski suits, corsets and suspenders -- items which the EU's main developing country trade partners are not usually associated with.
Last month European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said the EU's offer would be modest unless major exporters showed willingness to liberalise their textile markets.
On Wednesday he made good that threat, although the Commission -- the EU's executive -- nevertheless presented its offer as a generous one.

"By eliminating a large number of quotas, the proposal will give the unequivocal signal to our textile trading partners that the European Union is fully committed to liberalising trade in textiles," said a statement from his office.
But it added: "The absence of the most sensitive products from the proposal is also due to the disappointing response ... from supplying countries."

Under the terms of a four-stage agreement to scrap tariffs, quotas and other barriers on textile trade by 2005, the EU is obliged this year to open its markets by a further 17 percent of 1990's volume.

Major developing world exporters -- particularly in Asia -- are not under any obligation to open their markets in this phase but the EU has been calling for some reciprocity in order to prevent a "big bang" liberalisation in 2005.
The Commission said its list of 24 different product categories includes 19 that are covered by one or more important quotas and makes up 17.84 percent of 1990's volume.

But it accepted that none of the quotas of the products were currently being exceeded. "The quotas eliminated represent only a portion of total imports and in most instances are used only partially," a spokesman said.

The Commission's list must be approved by EU foreign ministers later this month so that it can come into effect by January 1. In the penultimate phase, the EU must reduce quotas by a further 18 percent by 2002.
Some EU countries -- notably Portugal, Spain and Italy -- have resisted attempts by the Commission to scrap quotas on certain textiles and garments in order to protect their industries.

A Commission spokesman said, however, that the latest round of cuts would have little effect on EU industry. "The sensitivity of industry and its regional impact on employment has been taken into account," he said.
The list will have little impact for developing countries. Generally, if quotas are underfilled, it is because the market is saturated or EU industry is competitive in that area.

But the Commission spokesman said scrapping the quotas -- which meant also that import licences are no longer needed for those products -- meant "developing countries would have an opportunity to demonstrate their dynamism and exploit a potential market".
The list of products on which quotas are being scrapped indludes gloves, carpets, swimwear, synthetic tights, tents, rope, shawls and carded or combed wool.
